blocks.x: Let's see, can we get your name again Mr. Lorycanner?
Yeah, now listen.
Your name is John William Lorycanner?
Yeah, I got two names. I don't know by the name of John, I don't know by the name of William, I don't know by the name of Bud.
Just B-U-D, Bud, huh?
Yeah.
Oh, I see. And when were you born?
Me?
Mm-hmm.
November 15th, 1879.
November the 15th, 1879.
Yeah, I'll be 80 years old next birthday.
Mm-hmm. And where were you born exactly?
New Orleans.
Were you born in the Channel or uptown or downtown?
No, I, no, I was born in the Magadine.
Mm-hmm. And what about your family? Were there any musicians in your family when you were born? Like your father, your uncles?
Yeah, my father was a guitar player.
Mm-hmm. And what was his name?
Jefferson.
Jefferson Lorycanner? Yeah. Mm-hmm. And what kind of music did he play?
Guitar.
Play just by note or by ear?
No, by ear.
Mm-hmm. And you remember any of the songs he played? No.
He got my dad. Mm-hmm.
Were they just regular popular songs or classical music or Italian?
Popular songs, yeah, popular songs. Mm-hmm.
Would he play what you call jazz on the guitar? No.
I would probably have a name of, of, uh, uh, uh, Ed DeBarra.
I couldn't get that name. Ed DeBarra.
Ed DeBarra.
Yeah.
Dead and better now.
It seems to me that, uh, Joe was telling me there were mostly Italians got together in that band?
Yeah.
Are you, you are, uh, the Lorycanners are Italian? Yeah, my father is.
My mother's Irish. Your mother's Irish and your father's Italian?
Yeah. A lot of people like that, uh, Tony Spavaro.
I think his mother's Irish and his father's Italian.

And, uh, what faith did they bring you up in? Catholic. Mm-hmm. Did you hear any music in church? No. Didn't have much music in church? No. The reason I ask is because it seems like they take the church music and jazz it up. Now, you know? Yeah, no. They're doing that to a lot of the old hymns. Never had none to that, I can remember.
They didn't do that in those days.
Uh, did any of your uncles play music? Yeah.
Yeah.
Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. Yeah.
Yeah. Yeah.
Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. Yeah.
Yeah. Yeah. Yeah.
No, Cousins. Cousins. What instrument was that?
Cousins. Joe, he played a chord in.
What was his last name?
Joseph. Joseph Lloyd Cannon. Joseph Lloyd Cannon.
Just like your brother. Yeah. Mm-hmm. Did he play any other instrument? I didn't know.
And, uh... My poetry go with him, you know. Oh, yeah. Even my poetry style together.
I guess he was a little older than you, your cousin Joe?
Oh, yeah. I guess so.
Now, what about your brothers? Uh... You're the oldest? Yeah.
I'm the oldest. Mm-hmm. And who came next?
Arnold. Mm-hmm.
Then Joe, and then Jeff.
Then Jeff?
Yeah. Wasn't there Jack who played too?
His name, he called him Jack, his name was Jeff.
Oh, I see. And, uh...
He was out of a couple of months. He was out in Chicago. Mm-hmm. And, uh...
What instrument did you play? Me? Mm-hmm.
When you started? Juice Hop. Juice Hop.
Yeah. What age? What age? What age?
What age?
What age? You were a young boy.
Yeah. Yeah. And, uh... And, uh... And, uh... And, uh... And, uh...
Juice Hop.
Juice Hop. Juice Hop. Yeah. What age were you when you took up the Juice Hop?
About ten years old.
Mm-hmm.

Took up the Juice Hop, then from Juice Hop and went to Harmonica. Mm-hmm. And from Harmonica I went to guitar. From guitar I went to manna. From manna I went to violin. From violin I went to tuba. Then I went to bass pedal. I was a whippin' Peter's punch on the bass pedal. I used to slap him. Like nobody's business.
How would you hold your hand when you did that? Left handed.
You play bass left handed?
Mm-hmm. I've never seen anybody do that but you're a woodman Japan. Cher-Wood-Man Japan. Mm-hmm.
You're saying Dan Hughes played at the Lyric, huh?
Yeah.
And you were there with him, huh?
Yeah. Played for Lou Rose. Remember Lou Rose?
Oh, yeah, that's right. Wasn't he the one who wanted to take you away?
No, uh-uh. Somebody else wanted to take it away.
Well, who played left-handed guitar?
Me.
Was you? And you strung it like a right-handed?
Yeah.
And you had to hit... How would you hit? In an upstroke? Oh, yeah. Lou Rose, huh? He had that chill.
Yeah. What is that? Cut the mouth and... And... Cut the mouth and...

segments.title: Confirming his name: Bud Loyacano
segments.summary: The interviewer confirms his name; he says he goes only by Bud.

segments.title: Birth in New Orleans in 1879
segments.summary: He was born November 15, 1879, in New Orleans, and will be 80 next birthday.

segments.title: His father Jefferson, a guitarist who played by ear
segments.summary: His father Jefferson played popular songs on guitar by ear, not jazz.

segments.title: Italian-Irish heritage, church and a band of Italians
segments.summary: Talk of Ed DeBarra, a band of mostly Italians, his Italian father and Irish mother, Catholic upbringing and no jazzed church music.

segments.title: Musical cousin Joe Loyacano
segments.summary: Asked about uncles, he names his older cousin Joe, who played a chord instrument and shared his style.

segments.title: His brothers Arnold, Joe and Jeff
segments.summary: He is the oldest, followed by Arnold, Joe and Jeff, also called Jack, who played and was once in Chicago.

segments.title: Learning instruments from jew's harp to bass, played left-handed
segments.summary: He began at about ten on the jew's harp, moved through harmonica, guitar, mandolin, violin and tuba to bass pedal, and played left-handed.

segments.title: Playing at the Lyric with Dan Hughes and Lou Rose; left-handed guitar
segments.summary: He played at the Lyric with Dan Hughes and for Lou Rose, and played a left-handed guitar strung right-handed.
